title: Dilucidationes super methodo elegantissima, qua illustris de la Grange usus est in integranda aequatione differentiali dx/√X = dy/√Y

deep.reconstruction:
Context: in E506 Euler re-derives, by Lagrange's 1766-69 method, the integrals of separated equations dx/√X ± dy/√Y = 0. In §47 he fixes how the arbitrary constant is written: choose the integral so that y=0 gives x=k. The integral then reads 'x combined with y equals k', which is the normalised addition law. This page collects the results for the degree-2 cases.

Theorem II (§49). The equation is dx/(a+bx+cx²) + dy/(a+by+cy²) = 0. Write s = x+y and p = xy. Euler gives three equivalent integrals:
- I: (b+cs)/(cp−a) = −(b+ck)/a.
- II: (as+bp)/(cp−a) = −k.
- III: (b+cs)/(as+bp) = (b+ck)/(ak).

In modern terms, factor a+bx+cx² = c(x−r1)(x−r2). The integral is the cross-ratio type invariant [(x−r1)(y−r1)]/[(x−r2)(y−r2)] = const. Equivalently it is the ratio of the two pencil members p − r_i s + r_i². Any ratio of two members of this pencil is a first integral. Euler's three forms are three such ratios, and III is the quotient of II by I. In effect this is a Möbius-type (multiplicative or additive) group law in disguise.

Theorem III (§50). The equation is dx/√(A+Bx+Cx²) − dy/√(A+By+Cy²) = 0. The integral is
−B(x+y) − 2Cxy + 2√(XY) = −Bk + 2√(AK), with K = A+Bk+Ck².
It is rearranged as B(k−x−y) − 2Cxy = 2√(AK) − 2√(XY).

Corollary (§51). Changing the sign of √Y gives the sum equation dx/√X + dy/√Y = 0. Its integral is B(k−x−y) − 2Cxy = 2√(XY) − 2√(AK).

These are the trigonometric/hyperbolic addition theorems written algebraically. They serve as the base cases that Theorem IV (next page) generalises to quartic X, as the degree-2 specialisation D=E=0.
errors: §51 as printed reads dx/√(A+Bx+Cxx) = dy/√(A+By+Cyy) = 0. The first '=' is a misprint for '+'. The stated integral (with +2√(XY) − 2√(AK)) is correct for the sum dx/√X + dy/√Y = 0. Check: A=1, B=0, C=−1 gives √X√Y − xy = √(1−k²), i.e. cos(arcsin x + arcsin y) = const.

All formulas on this page check out. Specifically: the three forms of Theorem II reduce to x=k at y=0, and each numerator and denominator lies in the pencil spanned by (x−r_i)(y−r_i), so each form is a genuine first integral. Theorem III checks with A=1, B=0, C=−1 (cos(arcsin x − arcsin y) = xy + √X√Y). Form I degenerates to a trivial constant identity when c=0, but Euler does not apply it there.
Not on this page: the next page's Theorem IV has '2√Ak' where '2√(AK)' is meant. Its first displayed integral divides by (x+y)² where (x−y)² is required, as Corollary I itself uses.

ideas.what: Normalising the arbitrary constant of the integral of dx/P(x) ± dy/P(y) = 0 by requiring x=k when y=0, so the integral becomes an explicit 'addition law' for k
ideas.modern_name: Addition theorem / formal group law normalised by the identity element
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (E251, E252, E261 and the Institutiones calculi integralis); group-theoretic reading much later
ideas.where_published: E251/E252 (Novi Comm. 6, 1761), Institutiones calculi integralis vol. 1 (E342), and this paper E506

ideas.what: Three equivalent rational integrals of dx/(a+bx+cx²) + dy/(a+by+cy²) = 0
ideas.modern_name: Möbius (projective) invariants of the Riccati-type separated equation; cross-ratio integral
ideas.where_published: Earlier sections of E506 and Euler's integral calculus

ideas.what: Algebraic integral of dx/√X ∓ dy/√Y = 0 for quadratic X
ideas.modern_name: Addition formulas for arcsin/arcsinh (genus-0 case of Euler's addition theorem)

deep.surprise_reason: This is a summary page restating, with a normalised constant, standard integrals of separated equations with quadratic denominators, which are well known from Euler's earlier work. It contains no new construction; the only notable item is a misprint in §51.
transcription_corrections: §51: the transcription correctly reproduces the printed '=' between the two differential terms. Mathematically it should read '+', i.e. dx/√(A+Bx+Cxx) + dy/√(A+By+Cyy) = 0.
§50 second form: the right-hand side is 2√(A(A+Bk+Ckk)) − 2√((A+Bx+Cxx)(A+By+Cyy)); the transcription is essentially correct.
